title: Hands-on Exercise 2A: First-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (1st-SPPA)
text:
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (SPPA) is the evaluation of the pattern or distribution of a set of points on a surface. The points may represent:

events such as crimes, traffic accidents, or disease onsets, or
business services (e.g., coffee shops and fast-food outlets) or facilities such as childcare centres and eldercare centres.

First-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (1st-SPPA) focuses on understanding the intensity or density of points across a study area. It examines how the distribution of points varies over space, essentially identifying trends or patterns in point density. This type of analysis deals with the individual locations of points and their distribution, without considering interactions between them.
This exercise uses spatstat to perform two commonly used 1st-order SPPA methods, applied to childcare centres in Singapore, and will focus on two specific questions:

Are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
If the answer is not, then the next logical question is: where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?

5 Importing and Wrangling Geospatial Data Sets
The code chunk below imports the Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) data set, transforms it to the SVY21 projected coordinate system, and retains only the fields needed for the analysis that follows:

mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaGEOJSON.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414) %>%
  select(REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C, geometry) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

The Southern Group subzone, and the Western Islands and North-Eastern Islands planning areas, are excluded, since these consist mainly of offshore islands with no childcare centres.

mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")

The cleaned boundary data set is saved as an .rds file so it can be reloaded directly in later sections without repeating the import and filtering steps.

write_rds(mpsz_cl, "data/mpsz_cl.rds")

Next, the Child Care Services data set is imported, transformed to the same coordinate reference system as mpsz_cl. Only the NAME field is retained, since address and administrative details are not required for the spatial point pattern analysis that follows.

childcare_sf <- st_read("data/ChildCareServices.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414) %>%
  select(NAME, geometry)

KML’s driver in GDAL flattens all attributes into a single Description HTML blob, so a KML import of this same data set would return only two fields — Name and Description. 5.1 Mapping the Geospatial Data Sets
With both mpsz_cl and childcare_sf confirmed to share the same coordinate reference system, a static map is prepared below to visualise their spatial patterns together.

tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(childcare_sf) +
  tm_dots()














TipReading the code



tm_shape() declares which dataset to draw, and the layer function that follows it determines how: tm_polygons() renders mpsz_cl as filled subzone boundaries, while tm_dots() renders childcare_sf as point markers. The + operator layers them onto the same map, boundaries first so the childcare points render on top.








Important



Both geospatial layers fall within the same map extent, confirming their coordinate values refer to the same spatial context. This is an important check before any geospatial analysis proceeds.


Alternatively, an interactive point symbol map can also be prepared using the code chunk below:

tmap_mode('view')
tm_shape(childcare_sf) +
  tm_dots()

tmap_mode('plot')







WarningSwitch back to plot mode



Remember to switch back to plot mode after viewing the interactive map. Each interactive map consumes a connection, and displaying too many interactive maps (more than 10) in a single document can cause issues when published on Netlify.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2A: First-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (1st-SPPA)
text:
6 Geospatial Data Wrangling
spatstat relies on its own specific data structures: ppp (planar point pattern) for point data, and owin for observation windows. This section converts mpsz_cl and childcare_sf from sf objects into ppp and owin objects.

6.1 Converting sf Data Frames to ppp Class
spatstat requires point event data in *ppp* object form. as.ppp() converts childcare_sf into this format:

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)

Next, class() verifies the object class of childcare_sf:

class(childcare_ppp)

[1] "ppp"


We can also take a quick look at the summary statistics of the newly converted ppp object by using summary().

summary(childcare_ppp)

Marked planar point pattern:  1925 points
Average intensity 2.417323e-06 points per square unit

*Pattern contains duplicated points*

Coordinates are given to 11 decimal places

marks are of type 'character'
Summary:
   Length  N.unique   N.blank Min.nchar Max.nchar 
     1925      1572         0         9        74 

Window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units
                    (33590 x 23700 units)
Window area = 796335000 square units








TipMark variables: NAME only



childcare_sf was trimmed to NAME and geometry back in section 5, since DESCRIPTION held no distinguishing information (the same constant string across all records) and the remaining address/hyperlink fields were irrelevant to spatial analysis. As a result, NAME is the only mark variable reported.








Important



The output above flags that the pattern contains duplicated points. Duplicated points are a common issue in spatial point pattern analysis, and worth taking seriously rather than glossing over. Many of the statistical methods used to analyse point patterns assume that points are distinct and non-coincident; when this assumption does not hold, the results can be misleading. Hence, this issue will be investigated below.




6.2 Checking for Duplicated Points
The summary() output above flags that childcare_ppp contains duplicated points. In spatstat, this refers to points sharing identical coordinates, not identical names. duplicated() is the function used to check for this, and it takes an argument called rule, which controls exactly what counts as a duplicate:

rule = spatstat (the default): a point counts as duplicated only if both its coordinates and its marks match an earlier point exactly.
rule = deldir: coordinates are compared using the same method as the deldir package, for consistency with functions like Delaunay triangulation that rely on it.
rule = unmark: only coordinates are compared, ignoring marks entirely.


rules <- c("spatstat", "deldir", "unmark")

duplicate_counts <- list()
for (rule in rules) {
  duplicate_counts[[rule]] <- sum(duplicated(childcare_ppp, rule = rule))
}

print(duplicate_counts)

$spatstat
[1] 1

$deldir
[1] 1

$unmark
[1] 187








Note



Under the strict spatstat rule, only 1 duplicate is found: two entries both named “Summer Montessori” registered at the exact same coordinates, which likely reflects the same centre appearing twice in the source data rather than two distinct centres. The deldir rule returns the same result, since it also compares coordinates using an equivalent matching logic.
The unmark rule tells a very different story: 187 points share their coordinates with another point when names are ignored. A closer inspection of these locations shows that one address hosts “Childcare @ The Enrichment”, “MindChamps Preschool @ Jurong West”, and “Safari House Preschool JW” together, while another pairs “Key Elementary Eduhouse” with a branch of “PCF Sparkletots Preschool”. These are not data-entry errors: they reflect real childcare centres, under different names and likely different operators, sharing the same building or block.
This distinction matters for how the duplication should be handled. A single true duplicate (the “Summer Montessori” case) could reasonably be removed as a data error. However, treating all 187 coordinate-sharing points as errors would be wrong, since it would delete genuinely distinct childcare centres simply because they operate from a shared address.








TipWhy the results differ sharply by rule



Under the strict spatstat rule, almost no points qualify as duplicates, since two centres would need identical coordinates and identical names. Under unmark, which checks coordinates alone, the count rises substantially. This gap reveals something specific about the data: many pairs of childcare centres share a building or address, but operate under different names — most likely different operators registered at the same location, rather than a single centre entered twice.


The unmark rule above shows that 187 points share a location with another point, but not how many points cluster at each shared address.
To exactly see which centres are involved, the coincident points can be extracted and inspected directly:

coincident_points <- duplicated(childcare_ppp, rule = "unmark")
coincident_coordinates <- childcare_ppp[coincident_points]
coincident_coordinates

Marked planar point pattern: 187 points
marks are of storage type  'character'
window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units




6.3 Resolving the Duplicates
Coincident points can be handled in a few different ways:







Approach
What it does




Delete the duplicates
Simplest option, but discards potentially valid, distinct centres


Attach duplicate count as a mark
Uses analytical methods that explicitly account for it


Apply jittering
Small random perturbation, so no two points occupy the exact same location



As identified earlier, the “Summer Montessori” pair shares both coordinates and a name, and most plausibly reflects the same centre entered twice in the source data, rather than two different centres. The remaining coordinate-sharing groups are a different case: distinct centres, under different names, that genuinely share a building or address. Treating both cases the same way would either wrongly discard real data, or wrongly preserve a data-entry error, so the two are handled separately.
Step 1: Removing the true duplicate
The true duplicate is removed first, using unique(), which by default removes a point only if both its coordinates and its marks exactly match a point that appeared earlier:

childcare_ppp_unique <- unique(childcare_ppp)
childcare_ppp_unique

Marked planar point pattern: 1924 points
marks are of storage type  'character'
window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units


This drops the point count from 1,925 to 1,924.






Note



Only the second “Summer Montessori” entry is removed; the first “Summer Montessori” entry, along with the other two distinct centres sharing that same address (“Pat’s Schoolhouse” and “Star Learners @ Yung Ho”) are all kept.


Step 2: Resolving the remaining coincident points
With the removal of the true duplicate, some locations still hold more than one point. rjitter() resolves this by applying a small, independent random displacement to every point in the pattern, so that no two points occupy the exact same location:

childcare_ppp_jit <- rjitter(childcare_ppp_unique,
                              retry = TRUE,
                              nsim = 1,
                              drop = TRUE)

To confirm that no coincident points remain after jittering:

any(duplicated(childcare_ppp_jit))

[1] FALSE


The jittered point pattern is saved as an .rds file for reuse in later analysis:

write_rds(childcare_ppp_jit, "data/childcare_ppp_jit.rds")

From this point onward, childcare_ppp_jit is used in place of childcare_ppp for the remainder of this exercise.


6.4 Creating owin object
When analysing spatial point patterns, it is a good practice to confine the analysis to a defined geographical area, such as Singapore’s boundary. In spatstat, an object called owin is specially designed to represent this polygonal region.
The code chunk below, as.owin() is used to covert mpsz_cl into owin object.

sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)
class(sg_owin)

[1] "owin"


The result above confirms that sg_owin is indeed an owin object, which can be displayed using plot() function:

plot(sg_owin)










6.5 Combining the Point Events and owin Objects
In the final step of data preparation, childcare_ppp_jit is clipped to sg_owin, keeping only childcare centres located within Singapore’s boundary:

childcareSG_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[sg_owin]

The output object combined both the point and polygon feature in one ppp object class as shown below.

childcareSG_ppp

Marked planar point pattern: 1923 points
marks are of storage type  'character'
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units








Note



Observation: From the result, it was noted that the point count drops from 1,924 to 1,923. A possible reason could be because rjitter() displaces each point within childcare_ppp_jit’s own rectangular window, which extends slightly beyond Singapore’s actual coastline. One point, likely sitting close to the original boundary, was jittered into that gap between the rectangle and the true polygon, landing just outside sg_owin.

section: 7 Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
text:
7 Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
Nearest Neighbor Analysis (NNA) is a spatial statistics method that calculates the average distance between each point and its closest neighbor to determine if a pattern of points is clustered, dispersed, or randomly distributed.
Clark-Evans test is a specific statistical method used within NNA to quantify whether a point pattern is clustered, random, or uniformly spaced, using the Clark-Evans aggregation index (R) to describe this pattern. NNA provides a numerical value that describes the degree of clustering or regularity, and the Clark-Evans test calculates a specific index (R) for this purpose.
In this section, the Clark-Evans test of aggregation for a spatial point pattern is performed using clarkevans.test() of the spatstat.explore package.
The test hypothesis are:

H0: The distribution of childcare centres is randomly distributed.
H1: The distribution of childcare centres is not randomly distributed.

A 95% confidence interval is used.
clarkevans.test() of spatstat.explore supports two variants of the Clark-Evans test: 1. Without CSR and 2. With CSR.

7.1 Performing the Clark-Evans Test Without CSR
The code chunk below uses the method without CSR:

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                 correction = "none",
                 clipregion = sg_owin,
                 alternative = c("clustered"))


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.55518, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








NoteStatistical conclusion



With R = 0.55518 (R < 1) and a p-value lower than the 0.05 level of significance, the null hypothesis is rejected. Childcare centres in Singapore are significantly clustered rather than randomly distributed.








TipTakeaway from statistical analysis



Childcare centres in Singapore are not spread out evenly across the island. Instead, they tend to cluster together in certain areas, likely reflecting where families and young children actually live. This pattern is strong and statistically conclusive, not a result of chance variation in the data.




7.2 Performing the Clark-Evans Test with CSR
The code chunk below uses method = "MonteCarlo". In this case, the p-value is computed by comparing the observed value of R to the results from nsim (i.e. 39, 99, 999) simulated realisations of Complete Spatial Randomness, conditional on the observed number of points:

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                 correction = "none",
                 clipregion = sg_owin,
                 alternative = c("clustered"),
                 method = "MonteCarlo",
                 nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.55518, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








NoteStatistical conclusion



With R = 0.55518 (R < 1) and a p-value of 0.01, below the 0.05 level of significance, the null hypothesis is rejected. This result is consistent with the earlier test without CSR, confirming that childcare centres in Singapore are significantly clustered rather than randomly distributed.








TipTakeaway from statistical analysis



Two independent methods (1. Without CSR and 2. With CSR) arrive at the same conclusion: childcare centres are not spread evenly across Singapore, but cluster together in certain areas. This consistency across methods adds confidence that the pattern is real, rather than an artefact of how the test was calculated.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2A: First-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (1st-SPPA)
text:
8 Kernel Density Estimation Method
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is a valuable tool for visualising and analysing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA), since it transforms discrete point data (such as childcare centre locations, crime incidents, or disease cases) into continuous density surfaces that reveal clusters and variations in event occurrence, without making prior assumptions about the underlying data distribution. It helps in understanding data distribution, identifying hotspots, and exploring relationships between spatial variables before more rigorous analysis is performed.
This section covers computing the kernel density estimation (KDE) of childcare centres in Singapore.

8.1 Working with Automatic Bandwidth Selection Method
The code chunk below computes a kernel density using the following configurations of density() of spatstat:

bw.diggle() as the automatic bandwidth selection method. Other recommended methods are bw.CvL(), bw.scott(), or bw.ppl().
The smoothing kernel used is gaussian, which is the default. Other smoothing methods are epanechnikov, quartic, or disc.
The intensity estimate is corrected for edge effect bias using the method described by Jones (1993) and Diggle (2010, equation 18.9). The default is FALSE.


kde_SG_diggle <- density(childcareSG_ppp,
                          sigma = bw.diggle,
                          edge = TRUE,
                          kernel = "gaussian")







Note



The output of density() of spatstat is an im class, representing a two-dimensional pixel image. It is used to store and manipulate raster data, where the spatial domain is divided into a grid of rectangular pixels. Each pixel has an associated value, which can be numerical or a factor.


The plot() function of Base R is then used to display the kernel density derived.

plot(kde_SG_diggle)








Below is a summary report of the derived kernel density surface:

summary(kde_SG_diggle)

real-valued pixel image
128 x 128 pixel array (ny, nx)
enclosing rectangle: [2667.538, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units
dimensions of each pixel: 416 x 225.0614 units
Image is defined on a subset of the rectangular grid
Subset area = 669941961.12307 square units
Subset area fraction = 0.437
Pixel values (inside window):
    range = [-5.782802e-21, 3.208627e-05]
    integral = 1925.947
    mean = 2.874797e-06








Important



The range above shows a maximum density of roughly 0.0000321 points per square metre. This is not because the pattern is sparse; it is a consequence of measuring density in SVY21’s base unit, metres. Singapore’s land area is roughly 700 million square metres, hence any density expressed per square metre produces very small decimal values regardless of how concentrated the actual points are. When expressed as points per square kilometre (multiplying by 1,000,000), the same maximum value reads as approximately 32.1, a more intuitive figure.


Before moving to the next section, the bandwidth used to compute the KDE layer can be retrieved using the code below.

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw

   sigma 
288.9242 




8.2 Rescaling KDE Values
rescale.ppp() converts the unit of measurement from metres to kilometres:

childcareSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcareSG_ppp, 1000, "km")

The rescaled data set is then passed into density() to recompute the kernel density surface, and plot() displays the result.

kde_childcareSG_km <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                               sigma = bw.diggle,
                               edge = TRUE,
                               kernel = "gaussian")

plot(kde_childcareSG_km)








The output image looks identical to the earlier version; only the data values change, as reflected in the legend.






TipResolving the earlier scale issue



Rescaling to kilometres directly addresses the readability problem flagged earlier: with distances measured in kilometres rather than metres, the resulting density values land in an easily interpreted range (the legend here runs from 0 to roughly 30), instead of the near-unreadable values per square metre.




8.3 Working with Different Automatic Bandwidth Methods
Besides bw.diggle(), three other spatstat functions can be used to determine the bandwidth: bw.CvL(), bw.scott(), and bw.ppl().
The bandwidth values returned by each method are compared below:

bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km)

    sigma 
0.2889242 



bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)

   sigma 
3.790548 



bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

 sigma.x  sigma.y 
2.159585 1.395526 



bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)

    sigma 
0.2738131 


Baddeley et al. (2016) suggested the use of the bw.ppl() algorithm because past experience showed that it tends to produce more appropriate values when the pattern consists predominantly of tight clusters. They also noted that if the purpose of the study is to detect a single tight cluster in the midst of random noise, the bw.diggle() method may work better.
The code chunk below compares the output of bw.diggle() and bw.ppl() methods:

kde_childcareSG_ppl <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                                sigma = bw.ppl,
                                edge = TRUE,
                                kernel = "gaussian")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")










8.4 Working with Different Kernel Methods
By default, the kernel method used in density.ppp() is gaussian. There are also three other options available: epanechnikov, quartic, and disc.
The code chunk below computes three more kernel density estimations using these three kernel functions:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
             sigma = 0.2889242,
             edge = TRUE,
             kernel = "gaussian"),
     main = "Gaussian")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
             sigma = 0.2889242,
             edge = TRUE,
             kernel = "epanechnikov"),
     main = "Epanechnikov")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
             sigma = 0.2889242,
             edge = TRUE,
             kernel = "quartic"),
     main = "Quartic")
plot(density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
             sigma = 0.2889242,
             edge = TRUE,
             kernel = "disc"),
     main = "Disc")

text:
9 Fixed and Adaptive KDE

9.1 Computing KDE Using a Fixed Bandwidth
A KDE layer is computed using a fixed bandwidth of 600 metres. Since the unit of measurement for childcareSG_ppp_km is in kilometres (600m = 0.6km), this is expressed as sigma = 0.6.

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                               sigma = 0.6,
                               edge = TRUE,
                               kernel = "gaussian")

plot(kde_childcareSG_fb)










9.2 Computing KDE Using Adaptive Bandwidth
The fixed bandwidth method is very sensitive to highly skewed distributions of spatial point patterns across geographical units, such as urban versus rural areas. One way to address this is to use adaptive bandwidth.
This section covers deriving adaptive kernel density estimation using adaptive.density() of spatstat.

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(childcareSG_ppp_km,
                                        method = "kernel")

plot(kde_childcareSG_ab)














TipWhy adaptive bandwidth handles this differently



A fixed bandwidth applies the same smoothing radius everywhere on the map, regardless of local point density. In a densely packed area, this can over-smooth and blur together clusters that are genuinely distinct; in a sparse area, the same fixed radius may be too narrow to reveal any pattern at all.
Adaptive bandwidth adjusts the radius locally: shorter in dense regions, longer in sparse ones, allowing it to represent both mature, densely built-up estates and newer, sparser ones more accurately within the same map.


The fixed and adaptive kernel density estimation outputs are compared using the code chunk below:

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")

11 First Order SPPA at the Planning Subzone Level
This section extends the analysis to the planning area level. For simplicity, the focus is on the Punggol, Tampines, Choa Chu Kang, and Jurong West planning areas.

11.1 Geospatial Data Wrangling

11.1.1 Extracting the Study Area
The code chunk below extracts the four target planning areas:

pg <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "PUNGGOL")
tm <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")
ck <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")
jw <- mpsz_cl %>%
  filter(PLN_AREA_N == "JURONG WEST")

The code chunk below plots each extracted planning area:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(st_geometry(pg), main = "Punggol")
plot(st_geometry(tm), main = "Tampines")
plot(st_geometry(ck), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(st_geometry(jw), main = "Jurong West")










11.1.2 Creating owin Objects
These sf objects are converted into owin objects, required by spatstat:

pg_owin <- as.owin(pg)
tm_owin <- as.owin(tm)
ck_owin <- as.owin(ck)
jw_owin <- as.owin(jw)



11.1.3 Combining the Point Events and owin Objects

childcare_pg_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[pg_owin]
childcare_tm_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[tm_owin]
childcare_ck_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[ck_owin]
childcare_jw_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[jw_owin]

*rescale.ppp()* is used to convert the unit of measurement from metres to kilometres:

childcare_pg_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_tm_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_jw_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_jw_ppp, 1000, "km")

The code chunk below plots the four study areas along with the locations of the childcare centres within each:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(unmark(childcare_pg_ppp_km), main = "Punggol")
plot(unmark(childcare_tm_ppp_km), main = "Tampines")
plot(unmark(childcare_ck_ppp_km), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(unmark(childcare_jw_ppp_km), main = "Jurong West")











11.2 Clark and Evans Test
Using clarkevans.test() of spatstat, the Clark-Evans test of aggregation is run on each of the four planning areas.
The hypotheses tested are:

H0: The distribution of childcare centres within the planning area is randomly distributed.
H1: The distribution of childcare centres within the planning area is not randomly distributed.


11.2.1 Punggol Planning Area

clarkevans.test(childcare_pg_ppp,
                 correction = "none",
                 clipregion = NULL,
                 alternative = c("two.sided"),
                 method = "MonteCarlo",
                 nsim = 999)

11.2.3 Choa Chu Kang Planning Area

                 correction = "none",

                 correction = "none",

Analysis of Results:
All four planning areas reject the null hypothesis of complete spatial randomness at the 0.05 significance level, with every R value falling below 1. Childcare centres are significantly clustered within each of the four areas individually.
Ranking the four by clustering strength (lowest R to highest): Tampines (0.690) shows the strongest within-area clustering, followed by Jurong West (0.722), then Punggol (0.847), with Choa Chu Kang (0.892) closest to random of the four.






TipTakeaway



Each of the four planning areas sits closer to 1 than the whole-of-Singapore result (R = 0.55518). This reflects two different scales of clustering, not a contradiction. The national test captures clustering between areas, since some planning areas simply have far more childcare centres than others. Restricting the test to a single planning area removes that between-area effect, leaving only the clustering that occurs within the area, at the neighbourhood level. This within-area signal is real and statistically significant.

7 Working with Projection
Map projection is an important property of a geospatial data. In order to perform geoprocessing using two geospatial data, we need to ensure that both geospatial data are projected using similar coordinate system.
This section covers how to convert a simple feature data frame from one coordinate system to another — a process known as projection transformation.

7.1 Assigning EPSG code to a simple feature data frame
One common issue that can happen during importing geospatial data into R is that the coordinate system of the source data is either missing (such as due to missing .proj for ESRI shapefile) or wrongly assigned during the import process.

8 Importing and Converting An Aspatial Data
In practice, it is not unusual to come across data such as listings from Inside Airbnb. This kind of data is referred to as aspatial data — it is not geospatial data, but among the data fields, there are two fields that capture the x- and y-coordinates of the data points.
This section covers how to import aspatial data into R and save it as a tibble data frame, before converting it into a simple feature data frame.

8.1 Importing the aspatial data
Since the listings data set is in csv file format, read_csv() function of readr package is used to import listings.csv, as shown in the code chunk below. The output R object is called listings, and it is a tibble data frame.

listings <- read_csv("data/aspatial/listings.csv")

8.2 Creating a simple feature data frame from an aspatial data frame
The code chunk below converts listing data frame into a simple feature data frame by using st_as_sf() of sf packages.

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(listings, 
                       coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                       crs=4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

A few things to note about the arguments above:

coords argument requires you to provide the column name of the x-coordinates first then followed by the column name of the y-coordinates.

9 Geoprocessing with sf package
Besides providing functions to handling (i.e. importing, exporting, assigning projection, transforming projection etc) geospatial data, sf package also offers a wide range of geoprocessing (also known as GIS analysis) functions.
This section covers how to answer real-world GIS questions using geoprocessing functions of sf package.

9.1 Use Case 1: Land Acquisition Analysis
Scenario:
The authority is planning to upgrade the existing cycling path. To do so, 5 metres of reserved land on both sides of the existing cycling path needs to be acquired. The task is to determine the extent of the land that needs to be acquired and its total area.
Solution:
Firstly, st_buffer() of sf package is used to compute the 5-meter buffers around cycling paths.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(
  cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

This is followed by calculating the area of the buffers as shown in the code chunk below.

buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)

Lastly, sum() of Base R will be used to derive the total land involved.

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]


A plot can also be created showing the buffer for a selected planning subzone - Tampines West is used as an example here.
Firstly, filter() of dplyr package will be used to extract polygon feature of Tampines West by using the code chunk below.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST") 

Next, st_intersection() of sf package will be used to clip cycling buffers within Tampines West planning subzone.

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(
  buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)

Finally, plot() of R Graphics is used to visualise the buffer clipped to the Tampines West subzone.

plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected))










9.2 Use Case 2: To determine the number of pre-schools by planning subzone
Scenario:
The authority requires a count of pre-schools for each planning subzone to support forward planning. The task is to compute these counts using geoprocessing functions of the sf package.
Solution:
The code chunk below performs two operations at once:

Identify pre-schools located inside each Planning Subzone by using st_intersects().
length() of Base R is used to calculate numbers of pre-schools that fall inside each planning subzone.


mpsz$`PreSch Count`<- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

Summary statistics of the newly derived PreSch Count field can be checked using summary(), as shown in the code chunk below.

10 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
This section covers how to visualise the derived variables using appropriate exploratory data analysis methods of ggplot2.

10.1 Distribution of pre-school density
A histogram can be used to reveal the distribution of PreSch Density. hist() of R Graphics is used:

hist(mpsz$`PreSch Density`)








Although the syntax is easy to use, the output falls short of publication quality. Furthermore, the function offers limited room for further customisation.
In the code chunk below, appropriate ggplot2 functions will be used.

ggplot(data = mpsz,
       aes(x = as.numeric(`PreSch Density`))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  labs(title = "Are pre-school evenly distributed in Singapore?",
       subtitle = "There are many planning subzones with a single pre-school, on the other hand, \nthere are nine planning subzones with at least 30 or more pre-schools",
       x = "Pre-school density (per km sq)",
       y = "Frequency")










10.2 Relationship between pre-school density and count
In the code chunk below, a scatterplot is used to show the relationship between Pre-school Density and Pre-school Count.

ggplot(data=mpsz, 
       aes(y = `PreSch Count`, 
           x= as.numeric(`PreSch Density`)))+
  geom_point(color="black", 
             fill="light blue") +
  xlim(0, 40) +
  ylim(0, 40) +
  labs(title = "",
      x = "Pre-school density (per km sq)",
      y = "Pre-school count")














Note



The scatterplot reveals a general positive relationship between pre-school density and pre-school count, where subzones with more pre-schools tend to have higher density.
However, the relationship is not strictly linear, particularly at lower density values, where subzones show a wide range of pre-school counts. This suggests that density alone does not fully capture how many pre-schools a subzone has, since it is also influenced by the subzone’s physical area.

text:
Thematic mapping involves the use of map symbols to visualize selected properties of geographic features that are not naturally visible, such as population, temperature, crime rate, and property prices.
Geovisualisation, on the other hand, is the process of using visual representations and cartographic techniques to explore, analyze, and communicate geospatial data. It combines elements of cartography, computer science, and information visualization to enhance spatial understanding and knowledge discovery.
This exercise explores how to create functional and truthful choropleth maps using the tmap package.

3.2 Importing Geospatial Data into R
The code chunk below uses the st_read() function of sf package to import Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) into R as a simple feature data frame called mpsz.

3.3 Importing Attribute Data into R
The respopagesextod2024.csv file is imported into a tibble dataframe called popdata, using read_csv() of the readr package.

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")



3.4 Data Preparation
Before a thematic map can be prepared, a data table with year 2024 values is required. The data table includes the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, and DEPENDENCY.

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 until age group 20 to 24
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25-29 until age group 60-64
AGED: age group 65 and above
TOTAL: all age groups
DEPENDENCY: the ratio between young and aged against the economy active group


3.4.1 Data Wrangling
The following data wrangling and transformation functions are used:

pivot_wider() of the tidyr package, and
mutate(), filter(), group_by(), and select() of the dplyr package


# Step 1: Group the data by PA (Planning Area), SZ (Subzone), and AG (Age Group)
popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG)

# Step 2: Summarise the data by calculating the total population (POP) for each group
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Step 3: Reshape the data from long to wide format, with age groups as column names
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP)

# Step 4: Calculate the YOUNG population (sum of selected age groups)
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6]) + rowSums(.[14]))

# Step 5: Calculate the ECONOMY ACTIVE population (sum of selected age groups)
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:13]) + rowSums(.[15]))

# Step 6: Calculate the AGED population (sum of selected age groups)
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(AGED = rowSums(.[16:21]))

# Step 7: Calculate the TOTAL population (sum of all age groups)
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[3:21]))

# Step 8: Calculate the DEPENDENCY ratio (ratio of YOUNG and AGED to ECONOMY ACTIVE)
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`)

# Step 9: Select the relevant columns to be retained in the final dataset
popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY)



3.4.2 Joining the attribute data and geospatial data
Before the georelational join, an extra step is required to convert the values in the PA and SZ fields to uppercase. This is necessary because the PA and SZ fields contain a mix of upper- and lowercase, while SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N are entirely uppercase.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ),
            .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

Next, left_join() of dplyr is used to join the geographical data and attribute table using planning subzone name, e.g. SUBZONE_N and SZ as the common identifier.

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                           by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))







Note



left_join() of dplyr is used with mpsz as the left data table, to ensure that the output will be a simple features data frame.



write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

4 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap
Choropleth mapping involves the symbolisation of enumeration units, such as countries, provinces, states, counties or census units, using area patterns or graduated colors. For example, a social scientist may need to use a choropleth map to portray the spatial distribution of aged population of Singapore by Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary.
Two approaches can be used to prepare thematic map using tmap, they are:

Plotting a thematic map quickly by using qtm().
Plotting highly customisable thematic map by using tmap elements.


4.1 Plotting a choropleth map quickly using qtm()
The easiest and quickest to draw a choropleth map using tmap is using qtm(). It is concise and provides a good default visualisation in many cases.
The following code draws a cartographic standard choropleth map.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")














Note



Code Explanation:

tmap_mode() with “plot” option is used to produce a static map. To enable interactive mode, “view” option should be used.
fill argument is used to map the attribute (i.e. DEPENDENCY).





4.2 Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
Despite the usefulness of qtm() in drawing a choropleth map quickly and easily, the disadvantage is that it makes aesthetics of individual layers harder to control. To draw a high quality cartographic choropleth map as shown in the figure below, tmap’s drawing elements should be used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics (DOS)", 
             position = c("left", "bottom"))








The following sub-sections cover the tmap functions used to plot these elements.

4.2.1 Drawing a base map
The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elemments such as tm_polygons(), tm_symbols(), tm_lines(), tm_raster(), and tm_text().
In the code chunk below, tm_shape() defines the input data (i.e mpsz_pop2024) and tm_polygons() draws the planning subzone polygons.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()














Note



By default, polygon areas are shaded light gray (gray85) and polygon borders are drawn in slightly darker gray (gray25).




4.2.2 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, the target variable, such as DEPENDENCY, is assigned to tm_polygons().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")














Note




The default interval binning used to draw the choropleth map is called “pretty”. A detailed discussion of the data classification methods supported by tmap is provided under sub-section 4.3.
The default colour scheme used is blues3 of ColorBrewer (covered in more detail under sub-section 4.4).
By default, missing values are shaded in grey.





4.2.3 Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and tm_border()
tm_polygons() is a wrapper of tm_fill() and tm_borders(). tm_fill() shades the polygons using the default colour scheme, and tm_borders() adds the boundaries of the polygon features onto the choropleth map.
The following code draws a choropleth map using tm_fill() alone.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Notice that the planning subzones are shaded according to their respective DEPENDENCY values.
tm_borders() adds the boundaries of the planning subzones, as shown below.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Notice that light-gray border lines have been added onto the choropleth map.
The fill_alpha argument is used to define transparency number between 0 (totally transparent) and 1 (not transparent). By default, the alpha value of the col is used (normally 1).
Beside fill_alpha, tm_borders() takes three other arguments:

col = border colour,
lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and
lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.


tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")











4.3 Data classification methods of tmap
Most choropleth maps employ some methods of data classification. The point of classification is to take a large number of observations and group them into data ranges or classes.
tmap provides a total ten data classification methods, namely: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks.
To define a data classification method, the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons() is used.

4.3.1 Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods
The code chunk below shows a quantile data classification that used 5 classes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








In the code chunk below, equal data classification method is used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the distribution of quantile data classification method are more evenly distributed then equal data classification method.
Comparing classification methods:
The following choropleth maps use different classification methods supported by tmap, to compare their differences.

SDEqualPrettyQuantileK-meansHclustBclustFisherJenks



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "sd", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "pretty", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "kmeans", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "hclust", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "bclust", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "fisher", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks", 
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

















Note



Observation:
Different classification methods produce noticeably different color patterns. Methods like equal and sd are heavily skewed by the outlier, compressing nearly all subzones into a single pale class. In contrast, methods like quantile and jenks adapt to the data’s actual spread, revealing much clearer spatial variation across subzones. Choosing the right classification method based on the data’s distribution is therefore crucial to avoid misleading choropleth maps.


Comparing number of classes:
The following choropleth maps use the same classification method (kmeans) with different numbers of classes (2, 6, 10, and 20), to compare differences in output.

n = 2n = 6n = 10n = 20



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "kmeans", 
                n = 2)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "kmeans", 
                n = 6)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "kmeans", 
                n = 10)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "kmeans", 
                n = 20)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

















Note



Observation:
Using different number of classes within the same classification method affects how much detail the map reveals. With n=2, the outlier dominates the classification, splitting subzones into just two broad groups with almost no visible variation among the majority. As the number of classes increases, finer distinctions emerge, revealing spatial clusters that were hidden at lower values of n. However, at very high values of n, adjacent shades become difficult to tell apart, and the added precision offers diminishing returns for visual interpretation.




4.3.2 Plotting choropleth map with custom breaks
For all built-in styles, category breaks are computed internally. To override these defaults, breakpoints can be set explicitly using the breaks argument of tm_scale_intervals(). In tmap, breaks include a minimum and maximum. As a result, n+1 elements must be specified in breaks to end up with n categories, with values in increasing order.
Before setting break points, it is good practice to check descriptive statistics on the variable.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 


With reference to the results above, break points are set at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90. In addition, a minimum and maximum are also required in the breaks vector, which are set at 0 and 100 respectively. The resulting breaks vector is c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00).

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











4.4 Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps either defined by the user or a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

4.4.1 Using ColourBrewer Palette
To change the colour, the preferred palette is assigned to the values argument.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the choropleth map is shaded in green.
To reverse the colour shading, add a “-” prefix.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








Notice that the colour scheme has been reversed.


4.4.2 Cartographic Furniture
Beside map style, tmap also provides arguments to draw other map furniture such as compass, scale bar and grid lines.
In the code chunk below, tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar(), tm_grid(), and tm_credit() are used to add compass, scale bar, grid lines and data sources onto the choropleth map.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))











4.5 Map Layout
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohensive map. It includes the map background, frame, typography, scale, aspect ratio, margins, and more.
The map layout can be customized using the tm_layout() function. This section covers the most often used arguments of this function, using the dependency choropleth map as an example.

4.5.1 Map Legend
In tmap, several legend options are provided to change the placement, format and appearance of the legend.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency Ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










4.5.2 Map Style
tmap allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed. They can be called by using tmap_style().
The code chunk below shows the natural style is used.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tmap_style("natural")








To restore the default style, the following code is used:

tmap_style("white")

text:
5 Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also referred to as facet maps, are composed of many maps arrange side-by-side, and sometimes stacked vertically. Small multiple maps enable the visualisation of how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time.
In tmap, small multiple maps can be plotted in three ways:

by assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments,
by creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange(), and
by defining a group-by variable in tm_facets().


5.1 Assigning multiple values to at least one of the aesthetic arguments
In this example, small multiple choropleth maps are created by assigning two variables to the fill aesthetic.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = 
      tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in(
        "right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", 
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")










5.2 Arranging multiple choropleth maps in a grid layout
In this example, multiple choropleth maps are created and tmap_arrange() is used to arrange them in a grid layout.

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                  item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")
                
agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024)+ 
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "quantile", 
              values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp=1, ncol=2)










5.3 Defining a group-by variable with tm_facets()
In this example, multiple small choropleth maps are created using tm_facets().

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) + 
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2, 
            ncols = 3,
            free.coords=TRUE, 
            drop.units=TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"), 
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

section: 7 Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
text:
7 Complementing Thematic Map with Statistical Chart
Maps and statistical charts complement each other by visually representing different aspects of the same data, offering a more comprehensive understanding. Maps excel at showing spatial relationships and geographical patterns, while charts effectively display numerical data, trends, and comparisons. Combining both allows for a more insightful and engaging data narrative, especially when dealing with spatial data that also has quantifiable characteristics.
With tmap, a statistical chart can be incorporated into the map visualisation using the fill.chart argument of map layers and legend chart feature, as shown in the code chunk below.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile", 
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








The following code further improves the visual representation by highlighting and labelling outliers on the choropleth map.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY)

outlier_vals <- stats$out

outlier_sf <- mpsz_selected[mpsz_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tm_shape(mpsz_selected) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile", 
            values = "brewer.blues"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(),
          fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_labels("SUBZONE_N", col = "red", size = 0.5) +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R
text:
8 Creating Interactive Map
Interactive maps let users actively explore and interact with the data they display. Unlike static maps, they support zooming in and out, panning across areas, clicking on locations for more information, and working with data overlays or visualisations, making the experience more dynamic and informative. tmap allows easy switching between static and interactive maps using tmap_mode(), enabling the view most suited to a given analysis.
Building on the code from section 7, the following code creates an interactive map.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)






The interactive map above is far from satisfactory. While free zooming encourages exploration, too much freedom can leave users disoriented within the map.
To address this, the set.zoom.limits argument can be used to limit how far users can zoom in or out, as shown below.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(region_selected, 
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name" = "SUBZONE_N", 
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12,14))

title: Hands-on Exercise 2B: Second-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (2nd-SPPA)
text:
Second-order Spatial Point Pattern Analysis (2nd-SPPA) examines the spatial relationships between points in a pattern, specifically focusing on how the presence of one point influences the location of others. It goes beyond simply describing the overall density of points (first-order effects) by investigating clustering, dispersion, or randomness at various spatial scales.
This exercise uses spatstat to discover the spatial point processes of childcare centres in Singapore, and will focus on two specific questions:

Are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed throughout the country?
If the answer is not, then the next logical question is: where are the locations with higher concentration of childcare centres?

5 Data Import and Preparation
Data import and preparation for this exercise reuse the objects prepared in Hands-on Exercise 2A: the cleaned boundary data (mpsz_cl) and the jittered childcare point pattern (childcare_ppp_jit). Both were saved there as .rds files and copied into this exercise’s own data folder. Full details of the import, CRS transformation, and jittering steps are available under the following Hands-on Exercise 2A sections:

Importing and Wrangling Geospatial Data Sets
Geospatial Data Wrangling

The code chunk below loads both objects, then extracts the same four planning areas used in Hands-on Exercise 2A — Punggol, Tampines, Choa Chu Kang, and Jurong West:

mpsz_cl <- read_rds("data/mpsz_cl.rds")
childcare_ppp_jit <- read_rds("data/childcare_ppp_jit.rds")

pg <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "PUNGGOL")
tm <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")
ck <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")
jw <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "JURONG WEST")

6 Analysing Spatial Point Process Using G-Function
The G-function measures the distribution of distances from an arbitrary point to its nearest neighbouring point. This section computes the G-function using Gest() of spatstat, and tests it against Complete Spatial Randomness using envelope().

6.1 Choa Chu Kang Planning Area

6.1.1 Computing G-function Estimation
The code chunk below computes the G-function using Gest() of spatstat:

G_CK <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border")
plot(G_CK, xlim = c(0, 500))














NoteInterpretation



The plot shows two lines: the empirical G-function (black line), representing the actual cumulative distribution of nearest-neighbour distances observed among childcare centres in Choa Chu Kang, and the theoretical CSR G-function (red dashed line), representing the expected distribution if childcare centres were randomly distributed with no clustering or dispersion.
The black line lies consistently above the red line across the observed range of distances. 7 Analysing Spatial Point Process Using F-Function
The F-function estimates the empty space function F(r), the probability that the distance from an arbitrary location (not a data point) to the nearest observed point is at most r. Unlike the G-function, where higher observed values indicate clustering, a lower observed F-function than expected under Complete Spatial Randomness indicates clustering — since clustered patterns leave larger gaps between clusters, empty space distances take longer to fill in.
This section computes the F-function using Fest() of spatstat, and tests it against Complete Spatial Randomness using envelope().

7.1 Choa Chu Kang Planning Area

7.1.1 Computing F-function Estimation
The code chunk below computes the F-function using Fest() of spatstat:

F_CK <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp)
plot(F_CK)














NoteInterpretation

The three empirical F-function estimates — Kaplan-Meier (black), border (red dashed), and Chiu-Stoyan (green dotted) - track closely together throughout, while the theoretical CSR line (light blue dash-dot) sits visibly above all three, with the gap widening noticeably from r = 150 onward. 9 Analysing Spatial Point Process Using L-Function
The L-function is a variance-stabilised transformation of the K-function, computed so that its theoretical value under Complete Spatial Randomness is a flat line at zero rather than a curve. This makes deviations from CSR easier to identify visually. An L-function above the CSR line indicates clustering, while a value below indicates dispersion.
This section computes the L-function using Lest() of spatstat, and tests it against Complete Spatial Randomness using envelope().

9.1 Choa Chu Kang Planning Area

9.1.1 Computing L-function Estimation
The code chunk below computes the L-function using Lest() of spatstat:

L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(L_ck, . -r ~ r,
     ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)")














NoteInterpretation



The observed L-function (black line) dips briefly below the theoretical CSR line (red dashed, flat at zero) at very short distances, before rising consistently above it for the remainder of the observed range, reaching around 50–60 when d = 700–800.
This matches the pattern seen in the G-, F-, and K-function plots for Choa Chu Kang shown earlier, all of which compared the observed pattern directly against the theoretical CSR line and showed clear separation from it, though the Monte Carlo simulation tests for these functions have generally not confirmed this separation as statistically significant. title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
A spatio-temporal point process (also called space-time or spatial-temporal point process) is a random collection of points, where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples of events include incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, or the occurrences of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis, or volcanic eruptions.
The analysis of spatio-temporal point patterns is becoming increasingly necessary, given the rapid emergence of geographically and temporally indexed data in a wide range of fields. A range of methods for this type of analysis has been developed and implemented in R over the past decade, and this exercise draws on several of them.
For this exercise, forest fire events recorded in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, Indonesia between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2023 are used to illustrate the methods, procedures, and interpretations of spatio-temporal point pattern analysis.
Two specific questions guide this analysis:

Do forest fire locations in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung show spatial and spatio-temporal independence?
If independence does not hold, where are the clusters concentrated, and during which periods do they occur?

10 Spatio-temporal Point Patterns Analysis: stpp methods
This section covers spatio-temporal point pattern analysis using functions from the stpp package.

10.1 Preparing the Spatio-temporal Point Process Object for stpp
Step 1: Extracting forest fire coordinates from the fire point events

coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

Step 2: Creating a data frame by combining the x- and y-coordinates and temporal event. Note that the temporal event must be in integer.

fire_df <- data.frame(
  x = coords[, 1],
  y = coords[, 2],
  t = fire_sf$DayOfYear
)

Step 3: Creating stpp spatio-temporal object as.3dpoints() is used to convert the data frame into an stpp spatio-temporal object.

fire_stpp <- as.3dpoints(fire_df)
class(fire_stpp)

[1] "stpp"


The result can be visualised below:

plot(fire_stpp)














Note



Analysis:
The xy-locations plot shows fire events split into two separate clusters, one over Bangka Island and a smaller one over Belitung and its nearby islands, with a clear gap between them where the sea separates the two.
The cumulative number panel shows the total fire count increasing slowly from January to May, then climbing sharply from around July to November, before levelling off toward the end of the year. This steep rise corresponds to the fire season identified in the earlier monthly maps and KDE surfaces.




10.2 Computing spatio-temporal K-function
STIKhat() from stpp is used to compute the space-time inhomogeneous K-function.

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)

The result can be visualised using plotK().

plotK(kbb_stik)








Note



Analysis:
No contour lines appear near the bottom-left of the plot (short spatial distance, short time lag), since the K-function values there fall below the lowest threshold shown. Contour lines begin to appear only at moderate distances and time lags, then fan out in a rippling pattern towards the top-right, with lines becoming more closely spaced as both u and v increase. This pattern is consistent with forest fire events in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung not being independent in space and time. A comparison against the theoretical K-function under spatial randomness would be needed to confirm this statistically.




10.3 Comparing observed and theoretical K-function values
While the contour plot visually suggests spatio-temporal clustering, a more rigorous check compares the observed K-function (Khat) against the theoretical K-function expected under complete spatial randomness (CSR) (Ktheo). A ratio greater than 1 indicates observed clustering exceeds what randomness alone would predict.

k_ratio <- kbb_stik$Khat / kbb_stik$Ktheo
summary(as.vector(k_ratio))

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  4.803   6.751   8.222  10.935  11.315 100.687 








Note



Analysis:
Every value in the Khat/Ktheo ratio exceeds 1, ranging from a minimum of 4.80 to a maximum of 100.69, with a median of 8.22. This confirms that forest fire events in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung are not spatially and temporally independent, the observed K-function consistently exceeds what would be expected under CSR, at every distance and time lag examined.
This answers the exercise’s first question: forest fire locations are spatially and spatio-temporally clustered, not independent. The second question, where and when fires tend to cluster, is addressed by the KDE surfaces from earlier sections: the density surfaces consistently showed the highest concentration of fire activity on Bangka Island’s western side, with intensity peaking during the July to October period.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4: Spatial Weights and Applications
text:
This exercise covers computing spatial weights in R and using them to derive spatially lagged variables.
A spatial weights matrix is the rule that decides which areal units count as neighbours of which, and how much weight each neighbour carries. Every measure of spatial autocorrelation is calculated from that rule, so changing it can change the result: a pattern that appears clustered under one definition of neighbourhood may not under another. The choice is part of the analysis rather than a step that precedes it.
The following will be covered during the exercise:

importing geospatial data with sf package,
importing an aspatial csv file with readr package,
performing a relational join with dplyr package,
computing contiguity-based, distance-based, and inverse-distance spatial weights with spdep package, and
deriving spatially lagged variables with spdep package.

5.3 Comparing Queen and Rook contiguity
Rook contiguity produces fewer links than Queen, with an average of 5.0 links per county compared to 5.09 under Queen. This is expected, since every Rook neighbour is also a Queen neighbour, a shared edge always implies at least a shared vertex, but the reverse does not hold.
The county-level neighbour lists make this concrete: Taoyuan has 11 neighbours under Queen and 10 under Rook, losing exactly one, Nan. Checking the shared geometry between the two counties confirms the contact is a single point rather than an edge, so it satisfies Queen contiguity but not Rook’s stricter requirement, exactly the case the two criteria are meant to distinguish. Xinhuang and Linxiang remain least connected under both criteria, showing that their isolation reflects their position on the map rather than an artefact of which contiguity rule is applied.


5.4 Visualising contiguity weights
A connectivity graph draws a line between points, not between whole polygon shapes, so each polygon first needs a single point to represent it. A centroid, the geometric centre of a shape, serves this purpose. Simply calling st_centroid() on the geometry column would return sf point objects, but the connectivity graph’s plotting function needs plain coordinate values in a two-column table instead, so an extra step is needed to get from one format to the other.
To do this, a mapping function is used: map_dbl() from purrr. A mapping function takes a function and applies it separately to every item in a list, then collects all the results together into one vector. Here, the list being worked through is hunan’s geometry column, which holds one polygon shape per county, and the function applied to each shape is st_centroid().
Longitude is extracted first:

longitude <- map_dbl(hunan$geometry, ~st_centroid(.x)[[1]])







Note



.x stands for whichever polygon is currently being processed as map_dbl() works through the geometry column one element at a time. st_centroid(.x) computes that polygon’s centroid, and [[1]] retrieves the first coordinate value, longitude, from the result.


Latitude is obtained the same way, differing only in which coordinate is retrieved:

latitude <- map_dbl(hunan$geometry, ~st_centroid(.x)[[2]])







Note



[[2]] retrieves the second coordinate value, latitude, from each centroid.

6 Computing Distance-based Neighbours
dnearneigh() of spdep identifies neighbouring region points based on their Euclidean distance, controlled by two separate arguments: a lower bound (d1) and an upper bound (d2).
If the coordinates are not projected (i.e., in latitude and longitude), whether provided as a spatial coordinates object or as a plain two-column matrix, with longlat = TRUE, the function will calculate great circle distances in kilometres, assuming the WGS84 reference ellipsoid.

6.1 Determining the cut-off distance
Firstly, the upper limit for distance band needs to be determined. This can be done through the following steps:

Return a matrix with the indices of points belonging to the set of the k nearest neighbours of each other by using knearneigh() of spdep.
Convert the knn object returned by knearneigh() into a neighbours list of class nb with a list of integer vectors containing neighbour region number ids by using knn2nb().
Return the length of neighbour relationship edges by using nbdists() of spdep. If the coordinates are projected, the function returns distances in the units of the coordinates; otherwise, in km.
Remove the list structure of the returned object by using unlist().


k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.57   38.01   39.07   44.52   61.79 








Note



The above output shows that the maximum first-neighbour distance is 61.79km. Using this value as the upper threshold gives certainty that all units will have at least one neighbour.




6.2 Computing fixed distance weight matrix
The maximum of the first-nearest-neighbour distances calculated above is the distance from the single most isolated county to its own nearest neighbour.

cutoff <- ceiling(max(k1dists))
cutoff

[1] 62


The derived cut-off is applied as the upper bound of the distance band, with the lower bound at 0:

wm_d <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, cutoff, longlat = TRUE)
wm_d

Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 88 
Number of nonzero links: 324 
Percentage nonzero weights: 4.183884 
Average number of links: 3.681818 








Note

The output shows that the average number of links is 3.681818 (the number of nonzero links (324) divided by the number of counties (88)). This means that, on average, each county has roughly 3.68 other counties within 62 km of its centroid.
This is noticeably lower than the 5.09 average links per county found under Queen contiguity. The comparison is meaningful because both are describing neighbourhood size for the same 88 counties, just defined in two different ways. Queen contiguity treats two counties as neighbours if their boundaries touch at all, no matter how long or short the shared edge is. The fixed-distance band works differently as it only counts a neighbour if the two centroids are close enough, regardless of whether the counties share a border. Hence, this is why some Queen neighbours do not qualify. A large county can border several smaller ones along its edge, but its centroid might sit far from theirs, too far to fall within the distance band, even though the two counties are clearly touching on the map.

6.3 Computing adaptive distance weight matrix
One of the characteristics of fixed distance weight matrix is that more densely settled areas (usually the urban areas) tend to have more neighbours while the less densely settled areas (usually the rural counties) tend to have lesser neighbours. This matters because a county’s lagged value is the average of its neighbours’ values. Averaging over more neighbours smooths that average, diluting the influence of any single neighbour’s unusually high or low value.
It is possible to control the numbers of neighbours directly using k-nearest neighbours, either accepting asymmetric neighbours or imposing symmetry as shown in the code below.
